summary.title: Writing a Game Boy Emulator in OCaml
summary.one_liner: Learn how the CAMLBOY project structures a Game Boy emulator in OCaml, using functors, GADTs, first-class modules, and ppx_expect test ROMs, then compiles it to run in the browser via js_of_ocaml.
takeaways: Structure an emulator with a clocked main loop where the timer and GPU catch up to CPU cycles.
Use module signatures with include and functors to make the CPU testable with a mock bus.
Model a typed instruction set with GADTs so read_arg returns uint8 or uint16 correctly.
Use mooneye-style test ROMs with ppx_expect snapshot tests for regression testing during exploratory development.
Compile the OCaml emulator to JavaScript with js_of_ocaml and the Brr library, then optimize it from about 20 FPS toward 60 FPS.
summary.summary: The author describes CAMLBOY, a Game Boy emulator written in OCaml that runs in the browser, and explains the design choices made while learning the language. The article covers the architecture (CPU, timer, GPU, bus, registers, cartridges), the main loop that keeps hardware in sync, and how signatures, functors, GADTs and first-class modules are applied in practice. It also describes integration testing with test ROMs and ppx_expect, compiling to JavaScript with js_of_ocaml, and the start of performance optimization. The page is partial, ending as the optimization section begins.
